title: HALE ALOHA CHURCH
spans: C 1800 KING KAMEHAMEHA I CONSTRUCTED BRICK HOUSE AT LAHAINA
1823 FIRST AMERICAN MISSIONARIES LANDED ON MAUI TO BEGIN WORK HERE.
1825 KING KAMEHAMEHA III LIVED AT LAHAINA MUCH OF THE TIME.
1831 LAHAINALUNA SEMINARY ESTABLISHED FOR TEACHING TEACHERS.
1834 LAHAINALUNA PRESS PRODUCED BOOKS IN HAWAIIAN LANGUAGE.
1830-60 LAHAINA, AS PORT OF CALL FOR SHIPS IN PACIFIC WHALING FLEET,
MEETING PLACE OF AMERICAN CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY.
1896 ROYAL RESIDENCE AND THE LEGISLATURE MOVED TO HONOLULU.

IN 1855 THE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH HAD SEVERAL MEETING HOUSES IN LAHAINA INCLUDING THE ONE WAI'ANAE CHURCH, THE LARGEST OF THESE, BUILT OF WOOD AND THATCH, WAS USED FOR SCHOOL AS WELL AS FOR CHURCH SERVICES. WHEN THIS BURNED IT WAS NOT REPAIRED. THE CHURCH DECIDED TO TEAR THIS STRUCTURE DOWN AND WAS ERECT A NEW BUILDING, IT WAS NAMED HALE ALOHA IN COMMEMORATION OF LAHAINA'S ESCAPE FROM THE SMALLPOX EPIDEMIC OF 1853.

THIS BUILDING, WITH WALLS OF CORAL STONE, WAS COMPLETED IN 1858 AND WAS USED FOR CHURCH MEETINGS FOR MANY YEARS. DURING THE EARLY SIXTIES A GOVERNMENT SCHOOL WAS CONDUCTED HERE, THEN AFTER A LONG PERIOD OF NEGLECT, THE BUILDING WAS COMPLETELY RENOVATED IN 1908 TO BE USED FOR ENGLISH-LANGUAGE CHURCH SERVICES AND AS A PARISH HALL. BY 1910 A BELL TOWER OF WOOD CONSTRUCTION HAD BEEN ADDED AND THE BUILDING CONTINUED TO BE USED AS A CHAPEL UNTIL WORLD WAR I. IN THE YEARS THAT FOLLOWED IT WAS AGAIN NEGLECTED AND ABANDONED.
RECORDED BY THE UNITED STATES NATIONAL PARK SERVICE

description: This sheet documents Hale Aloha Church in Lahaina, Maui, Hawaii, as part of the Historic American Buildings Survey. It features a regional map of the Island of Maui and a detailed site plan of Lahaina showing street layouts and adjacent structures. The sheet includes extensive historical text describing the church's construction from coral stone in 1855 and its subsequent use and decline. Credits acknowledge the National Park Service, Lahaiana Restoration Foundation, and student architects from Texas A&M, University of Hawaii, and Kansas State University.
